questions.stem:
Statements: Some A are B. All B are C.
Conclusions: I. Some A are C. II. All C are A.
questions.explanation: A is correct. Some A → B (partial link). All B ⊆ C. Therefore: those 'some A' that are B are also C → some A are C (I ✓). Conclusion II 'All C are A' would require all C to come from A — but C includes B plus possibly more; B is a subset of C, and only SOME A are B. II ✗. Only I follows.

questions.stem:
Statements: No M is N. All N are O.
Conclusions: I. No M is O. II. Some O are not M.
questions.explanation: B is correct. No M is N (M and N are mutually exclusive). All N ⊆ O. The N elements are in O and are NOT M → some O (the N elements) are not M (II ✓). Conclusion I: No M is O — this would require M and O to be completely separate. But O might contain elements outside of N, which could overlap with M. I ✗. Only II follows.

questions.stem:
Statements: All dogs are animals. All wolves are dogs.
Conclusions: I. All wolves are animals. II. All animals are wolves.
questions.explanation: A is correct. Chain: wolves ⊆ dogs ⊆ animals. Conclusion I: All wolves are animals — TRUE (subset-subset transitivity ✓). Conclusion II: All animals are wolves — FALSE (animals is a much larger category than wolves; illegal conversion of 'All A are B' to 'All B are A'). Only I follows.

questions.stem:
Statements: Some politicians are honest. No honest person is corrupt.
Conclusions: I. Some politicians are not corrupt. II. No politician is corrupt.
questions.explanation: A is correct. Some politicians are honest (subset). No honest person is corrupt. Those 'some honest politicians' cannot be corrupt → some politicians are not corrupt (I ✓). But there may be OTHER politicians who are NOT honest, and those could be corrupt or not — we don't know. 'No politician is corrupt' (II) is too strong. Only I follows.

questions.stem:
Statements: All stones are hard. Some hard things are cold.
Conclusions: I. Some stones are cold. II. Some cold things are hard.
questions.explanation: B is correct. All stones ⊆ hard. Some hard ∩ cold ≠ ∅. Conclusion I: 'Some stones are cold' — the hard-cold intersection might not include any stones (only hard-non-stone objects might be cold). I ✗. Conclusion II: 'Some cold things are hard' — if some hard things are cold, then those cold things are hard (conversion of 'some' statement is always valid). II ✓. KEY: Converting 'Some A are B' → 'Some B are A' is ALWAYS valid.

questions.stem:
Statements: No book is a pen. Some pens are watches.
Conclusions: I. Some watches are not books. II. No watch is a book.
questions.explanation: A is correct. No book is a pen (B∩P = ∅). Some pens are watches (P∩W ≠ ∅). Those pens that are watches are NOT books (since no book is a pen, and these are pens). So some watches (the pen-watches) are not books → I ✓. For II 'No watch is a book': watches might include things that are also books (watches not from the pen category). II ✗. Only I follows.

questions.stem:
Statements: All circles are squares. All squares are triangles.
Conclusions: I. All circles are triangles. II. At least some triangles are circles.
questions.explanation: C is correct. Chain: circles ⊆ squares ⊆ triangles. I: All circles are triangles — TRUE (transitive chain ✓). II: Some triangles are circles — TRUE (since all circles are a subset of triangles, at least those circles are triangles, making 'some triangles = circles' valid ✓). Both follow.

questions.stem:
Statements: Some cups are bowls. Some bowls are plates.
Conclusions: I. Some cups are plates. II. No cup is a plate.
questions.explanation: C is correct. KEY RULE: Some A + Some B → No definite conclusion. The 'some cups' that are bowls may not be the 'some bowls' that are plates. So: cups might or might not be plates — we can't conclude either I or II. This is the classic 'Some + Some = Cannot conclude' rule. Neither follows.

questions.stem:
Statements: All tables are chairs. No chair is a bed.
Conclusions: I. No table is a bed. II. Some beds are chairs.
questions.explanation: A is correct. tables ⊆ chairs (all tables are chairs). No chair is a bed (chairs ∩ beds = ∅). Since tables ⊆ chairs and chairs ∩ beds = ∅, it follows that tables ∩ beds = ∅ → No table is a bed (I ✓). Conclusion II 'some beds are chairs' directly contradicts 'no chair is a bed' — II ✗. Only I follows.

questions.stem:
Statements: All trains are fast. Some fast things are buses.
Conclusion: Some buses are fast.
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Some fast things are buses' directly converts to 'Some buses are fast' — this is the simple conversion of a 'Some' statement: 'Some A are B' → 'Some B are A' (always valid). The conclusion 'Some buses are fast' FOLLOWS. The first statement (all trains are fast) is not even needed for this conclusion.
